Literal Sense

The Angels Arrive at Sodom

Genesis 19 opens with the arrival of two angels at Sodom in the evening. Lot, sitting at the gate of the city (a place of civic importance indicating his status as a resident of some standing), rises to meet them, bows with his face to the ground, and offers them hospitality: "And the two angels came to Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom" (Gen 19:1). Like his uncle Abraham in the previous chapter, Lot recognizes the dignity of his visitors and extends generous hospitality.

St. John Chrysostom, in his Homilies on Genesis, draws attention to Lot's imitation of Abraham's hospitality:

"Let us listen, dearly beloved, with caution and great fear to the contents of the divine Scriptures; there is nothing written there idly and to no purpose; instead, everything is said carefully and to our advantage, even if we do not understand parts of it. You see, we cannot understand everything precisely; on the contrary, even if we try to assign causes for some things to the extent possible to us, yet it still holds within it some treasure that is hidden and difficult to interpret."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, 44

The angels initially decline Lot's invitation, saying they will spend the night in the street, but Lot presses them urgently until they agree to enter his house. He prepares a feast for them, including unleavened bread. The urgency of Lot's invitation suggests his awareness of the dangers strangers faced in Sodom.

The Sin of the Sodomites

Before the household retires, the men of Sodom surround Lot's house, demanding that he bring out his guests so they might "know" them: "And they called Lot, and said to him: Where are the men that came in to thee at night? bring them out hither that we may know them" (Gen 19:5). The Hebrew word yada (to know) here carries the meaning of carnal knowledge, as confirmed by the narrative context and the tradition of interpretation.

St. Augustine, in The City of God, addresses the nature of Sodom's sin:

"The men of Sodom were driven by unnatural lust and attempted to violate even the angels who had come in the form of men. Their wickedness had cried out to heaven, and God came down to see whether their deeds matched the outcry that had reached Him."

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.30

The prophet Ezekiel provides additional context for Sodom's sins: "Behold this was the iniquity of Sodom thy sister, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance, and the idleness of her, and of her daughters: and they did not put forth their hand to the needy, and to the poor" (Ezek 16:49). The Fathers recognized a complex of sins in Sodom: pride, luxury, inhospitality, and sexual violence.

Lot's Attempt to Protect His Guests

Lot goes out to the men and shuts the door behind him, pleading with them not to act wickedly. In a deeply troubling passage, he offers his two virgin daughters to the mob instead: "I have two daughters who as yet have not known man: I will bring them out to you, and abuse you them as it shall please you, so that you do no evil to these men, because they are come in under the shadow of my roof" (Gen 19:8).

This offer has perplexed commentators throughout history. The Fathers generally understood it as reflecting the extreme importance of hospitality in the ancient Near East, while not condoning Lot's specific proposal. St. John Chrysostom observes that Lot was attempting to divert the men from a greater sin to a lesser one, though the offer itself was sinful. The angels intervene before any harm comes to either the daughters or themselves.

The Blinding of the Sodomites

The men of Sodom reject Lot's offer and threaten him, pressing against the door. The angels pull Lot inside and strike the attackers with blindness: "And they struck them with blindness from the least to the greatest, so that they could not find the door" (Gen 19:11). This supernatural intervention demonstrates the divine power of the messengers and foreshadows the judgment about to fall.

The Warning and Escape

The angels urge Lot to gather his family and flee, for they have been sent to destroy the city. Lot warns his sons-in-law, who were betrothed to his daughters, but they think he is joking. At dawn, the angels urgently press Lot to leave with his wife and two daughters. When he lingers, they grasp his hand and the hands of his family members: "And as he lingered, they took his hand, and the hand of his wife, and the hands of his two daughters, because the Lord spared him" (Gen 19:16).

Lot requests permission to flee to a nearby small city rather than to the mountains, fearing he cannot reach them in time. The angels grant this request, and the city is spared for Lot's sake and named Zoar (meaning "small"): "Behold also I have heard thy prayers concerning this thing, not to destroy the city for which thou hast spoken. Make haste and be saved there" (Gen 19:21-22).

The Destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah

When the sun rises over the land and Lot enters Zoar, the Lord rains brimstone and fire upon Sodom and Gomorrah: "And the Lord rained upon Sodom and Gomorrha brimstone and fire from the Lord out of heaven. And he destroyed these cities, and all the country about, all the inhabitants of the cities, and all things that spring from the earth" (Gen 19:24-25).

The phrase "from the Lord out of heaven" emphasizes the divine origin of this judgment. The destruction was total: the cities, the surrounding region, all inhabitants, and even the vegetation were consumed. Archaeological investigations near the Dead Sea have identified possible sites, with evidence of sudden destruction and sulfurous deposits.

Lot's Wife

Despite the explicit command not to look back, Lot's wife turns to gaze upon the destruction and is transformed into a pillar of salt: "And his wife looking behind her, was turned into a pillar of salt" (Gen 19:26). The Jewish historian Josephus claimed to have seen this pillar, as did the early Church Fathers Clement of Rome and Irenaeus.

St. Clement of Rome, writing in the first century, provides the earliest Christian commentary on this event:

"For his hospitality and godliness Lot was saved from Sodom, when all the country round about was judged by fire and brimstone; the Master having thus foreshown that He forsaketh not them which set their hope on Him, but appointeth unto punishment and torment them which swerve aside. For when his wife had gone forth with him, being otherwise-minded and not in accord, she was appointed for a sign hereunto, so that she became a pillar of salt unto this day, that it might be known unto all men that they which are double-minded and they which doubt concerning the power of God are set for a judgment and for a token unto all the generations."

St. Clement of Rome, First Epistle to the Corinthians, 11

Lot and His Daughters

The final section of Genesis 19 recounts the troubling episode of Lot and his daughters. After Sodom's destruction, Lot becomes afraid to remain in Zoar and withdraws with his daughters to a cave in the mountains. His daughters, believing themselves to be the last survivors of humanity, devise a plan to preserve their father's line by making him drunk and lying with him on successive nights.

The elder daughter conceives first, and then the younger. Neither time is Lot aware of what has happened: "And the elder bore a son, and she called his name Moab: he is the father of the Moabites unto this day. The younger also bore a son, and she called his name Ammon, that is, the son of my people: he is the father of the Ammonites unto this day" (Gen 19:37-38).

Origen, in his Homilies on Genesis, addresses this difficult passage:

"The daughters of Lot believed that the whole world had perished. They had heard that the world would end by fire, and when they saw fire raining down upon Sodom, they believed that they were the only human beings left to survive. So, out of necessity, they lay with their father so that the human race would not be destroyed. Scripture neither applauds nor condemns their actions, but relates them as they happened."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, V
allegorical:
Allegorical Sense

Sodom as a Type of the World Under Judgment

Throughout Scripture, Sodom and Gomorrah serve as types of the world under divine judgment. The cities represent human civilization in rebellion against God, prosperous in material goods but corrupt in spirit. Their destruction prefigures the final judgment that awaits all who persist in unrepentant wickedness.

The Apostle Peter makes this typological connection explicit:

"Turning the cities of the Sodomites, and of the Gomorrhites, into ashes, condemned them to be overthrown, making them an example to those that should after act wickedly."

2 Peter 2:6 (Douay-Rheims)

Similarly, Jude draws the parallel between Sodom and eschatological punishment:

"As Sodom and Gomorrha, and the neighbouring cities, in like manner, having given themselves to fornication, and going after other flesh, were made an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire."

Jude 1:7 (Douay-Rheims)

Lot as a Type of the Righteous Delivered from Judgment

Lot represents the righteous remnant whom God preserves from destruction. Though dwelling in the midst of wickedness, he maintained his integrity (as Peter calls him "just Lot" in 2 Peter 2:7) and was delivered when judgment fell. This typifies the deliverance of the faithful at the end of time, when Christ will gather His elect before the final conflagration.

St. Augustine, in The City of God, notes that Abraham's intercession secured Lot's deliverance:

"God remembered Abraham and delivered Lot from the destruction of the cities. Thus we see that the prayers of the righteous avail much for those who are connected with them, even when those others dwell among the wicked."

St. Augustine, City of God, XVI.29

The Angels as Ministers of Judgment and Salvation

The two angels who execute judgment on Sodom while simultaneously rescuing Lot prefigure the dual role of angels at the end of time. At the final judgment, angels will both gather the elect and execute judgment on the wicked: "So shall it be at the end of the world. The angels shall go out, and shall separate the wicked from among the just" (Matt 13:49).

Cyril of Alexandria, in his Glaphyra on Genesis, sees Christ Himself as the active agent of divine judgment prefigured in this narrative:

"The Son is plainly at the center of the Old Testament text, making him the active agent of judgment when God burned a city to the ground. For the Father has given all judgment to the Son, and what we see in Sodom is a type of the judgment Christ will execute at the end of the ages."

St. Cyril of Alexandria, Glaphyra on the Pentateuch

Lot's Wife as a Figure of Attachment to the World

Lot's wife, transformed into a pillar of salt for looking back at Sodom, represents the soul that, though outwardly departing from sin, remains inwardly attached to the pleasures and goods of this passing world. Our Lord Himself draws this moral lesson:

"Remember Lot's wife. Whosoever shall seek to save his life, shall lose it: and whosoever shall lose it, shall preserve it."

Luke 17:32-33 (Douay-Rheims)

St. Irenaeus of Lyons offers a striking ecclesiological interpretation:

"Though Lot's wife remains as a pillar of salt, she became an emblem of the true Church, which, though she suffers much and often loses whole members, yet preserves the pillar of salt, that is, the foundation of the true faith."

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies, IV.31

The Two Daughters as Types of the Two Churches

The most remarkable allegorical interpretation of the final episode comes from St. Irenaeus, who sees in Lot's two daughters a type of the two churches (or synagogues) that would spring from one father:

"This happened without Lot's knowledge and without his having been a slave to pleasure; it was accomplished wholly by divine arrangement, through which the two synagogues, born from one and the same father, without carnal pleasure, were evoked. For there was no one else that could give them vital seed and the fruit of children, as it was written. Since, therefore, Lot knew not what he did, nor was a slave to lust, the arrangement designed by God was carried out, by which the two daughters, that is, the two churches, who gave birth to children begotten of one and the same father, were pointed out, apart from the influence of the lust of the flesh."

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, Against Heresies, IV.31

In this typological reading, Lot represents God the Father, and the two daughters represent the Jewish and Gentile churches, both of which receive spiritual life from the same divine source. The offspring, Moab and Ammon, despite their troubled origins, would eventually contribute to the lineage of Christ through Ruth the Moabitess.

The Fire from Heaven as a Type of Final Judgment

The brimstone and fire that consumed Sodom prefigure the final conflagration at the end of time. As Peter writes: "But the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of the ungodly men" (2 Pet 3:7). The destruction of Sodom by fire from heaven is a prototype of this eschatological judgment.

Zoar as a Figure of Refuge

The small city of Zoar, spared from destruction for Lot's sake, represents the places of refuge that God provides for His people in times of judgment. Just as Lot found safety in this small city, so the faithful find refuge in the Church, the "little flock" to whom the Father has given the kingdom (Luke 12:32). The very name Zoar, meaning "small" or "insignificant," suggests that God's salvation often works through humble and overlooked means.

Hospitality and the Reception of Christ

Lot's hospitality to the angels, like Abraham's in the previous chapter, represents the soul's reception of divine grace. Those who welcome the messengers of God, even when they come in humble or unrecognized form, receive salvation. Those who reject them, like the men of Sodom, bring judgment upon themselves. This prefigures Christ's words: "He that receiveth you, receiveth me: and he that receiveth me, receiveth him that sent me" (Matt 10:40).
moral:
Moral Sense

The Gravity of Sin and Divine Justice

Genesis 19 presents a sobering picture of sin's consequences. The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah demonstrates that God's patience has limits, and that persistent, unrepentant wickedness eventually meets divine judgment. The sins of Sodom were manifold: pride, abundance without charity, neglect of the poor, and violent sexual perversion.

The prophet Ezekiel lists the moral failures of Sodom: "Behold this was the iniquity of Sodom thy sister, pride, fulness of bread, and abundance, and the idleness of her, and of her daughters: and they did not put forth their hand to the needy, and to the poor. And they were lifted up, and committed abominations before me" (Ezek 16:49-50). The moral lesson is that material prosperity without spiritual virtue leads to moral corruption and ultimate ruin.

The Virtue of Hospitality

Lot's hospitality stands in sharp contrast to the violence of the Sodomites. His urgent invitation to the strangers, his provision for their needs, and his willingness to protect them at great personal cost exemplify the virtue of welcoming the stranger. St. Ambrose of Milan draws attention to this contrast:

"Abraham, ready to receive strangers, faithful towards God, devoted in ministering, quick in his service, saw the Trinity in a type; he added religious duty to hospitality, when beholding Three he worshipped One. Lot, his nephew, shared in this hospitality, though his offering cannot compare with the feast of the fatted calf that Abraham offered his guests."

St. Ambrose of Milan, On Abraham

The New Testament explicitly draws the moral lesson: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb 13:2). In a world that often treats strangers with suspicion or hostility, the example of Lot and Abraham calls Christians to radical hospitality.

The Danger of Double-Mindedness

Lot's wife serves as a perpetual warning against spiritual double-mindedness. Though she physically left Sodom, her heart remained attached to what she left behind. St. Clement of Rome draws this moral lesson with great clarity:

"When his wife had gone forth with him, being otherwise-minded and not in accord, she was appointed for a sign hereunto, so that she became a pillar of salt unto this day, that it might be known unto all men that they which are double-minded and they which doubt concerning the power of God are set for a judgment and for a token unto all the generations."

St. Clement of Rome, First Epistle to the Corinthians, 11

The moral application is clear: those who begin the journey of faith must not look back with longing to their former way of life. As our Lord taught: "No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Luke 9:62). Lot's wife stands forever as salt, preserving the memory of this warning for all generations.

The Urgency of Repentance

The angels' urgent commands to Lot and his family emphasize the necessity of immediate response to God's call. There was no time for deliberation, no opportunity for delay. The moral lesson is that when God calls us to repentance and conversion, we must respond without hesitation. As Scripture warns: "Today if you shall hear his voice, harden not your hearts" (Heb 3:15).

Lot's lingering, despite the urgency of the situation, required the angels to physically grasp his hand and lead him out. How often do we also linger in our sins, requiring divine intervention to pull us away from destruction? The mercy shown to Lot in his hesitation gives hope, but it also warns against presuming upon that mercy.

The Defense of Lot's Daughters

The episode of Lot and his daughters has troubled readers throughout history. However, the Church Fathers generally offer an interpretation that, while not condoning the act, seeks to understand the circumstances that led to it. St. John Chrysostom provides pastoral guidance on how to read such difficult passages:

"Therefore, let no one ever presume to condemn the just man or his daughters. After all, how could it be other than a mark of extreme folly and stupidity on our part, laden as we are with such countless burdens of sin, to condemn those whom Sacred Scripture discharges of all sin and for whom rather it even supplies such a remarkable defense."

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies on Genesis, 44

The daughters believed themselves to be the last survivors of humanity. Having witnessed the destruction of Sodom and the transformation of their mother, they genuinely thought the world had ended. St. Ephrem the Syrian portrays their psychological state with sympathy:

"Lot and his daughters were terrified and grief-stricken, thinking they were the only people left in the world. Lot drinking wine was a way to get himself to sleep due to his anxiety after witnessing the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah and the turning of his wife into salt. Wine consoles old age; conception consoles youth."

St. Ephrem the Syrian, Hymns on Virginity, 38

Origen further explains that the daughters' motivation was not lust but the preservation of humanity:

"Lot's daughters believed that the entire world had been destroyed. They had heard that the world would end by fire so, when they saw the fire raining down on Sodom, they believed that they were the only human beings to survive. So, out of necessity, they slept with their father so that the human race would not be destroyed."

Origen, Homilies on Genesis, V

The moral lesson Origen draws is instructive: sexual union should be ordered toward procreation, not mere pleasure. Once the daughters had conceived, they did not return to their father. Their error was not in their motivation but in their judgment of the situation.

The Danger of Dwelling Among the Wicked

Lot's choice to dwell in Sodom, attracted by its material prosperity, brought him and his family to the brink of destruction. Though he maintained his righteousness, his extended residence among the wicked nearly cost him everything. The moral warning is clear: while we must live in the world, we must not allow ourselves to become so entangled in it that we cannot leave when God calls.

St. Peter describes Lot's inner torment: "And delivered just Lot, oppressed by the injustice and lewd conversation of the wicked. For in sight and hearing he was just: dwelling among them, who from day to day vexed the just soul with unjust works" (2 Pet 2:7-8). Lot's soul was daily vexed by the wickedness around him, yet he remained. How much better to remove oneself entirely from occasions of sin!

The Value of Intercessory Prayer

Though Abraham's intercession (Genesis 18) could not save Sodom itself, it secured Lot's deliverance. The text explicitly notes: "And when God destroyed the cities of that country, remembering Abraham, he delivered Lot out of the destruction of the cities wherein he had dwelt" (Gen 19:29). The moral lesson is that the prayers of the righteous benefit others, often in ways unknown. We should never cease to intercede for those in spiritual danger, trusting that God hears and remembers.
anagogical:
Anagogical Sense

The Destruction of Sodom and the Final Judgment

The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah stands throughout Scripture as the premier type of eschatological judgment. Our Lord Himself repeatedly points to these cities as warnings of the judgment to come. The characteristics of Sodom's destruction prefigure the final judgment in multiple ways.

The suddenness of the judgment is emphasized by Christ:

"As it was in the days of Lot: they did eat and drink, they bought and sold, they planted and built. And in the day that Lot went out of Sodom, it rained fire and brimstone from heaven, and destroyed them all. Even thus shall it be in the day when the Son of man shall be revealed."

Luke 17:28-30 (Douay-Rheims)

The scholarly investigation of this typology confirms its eschatological significance:

"The destruction of Sodom is seen as a prototype of eschatological divine judgment upon wicked cities, nations, or peoples with regard to its suddenness and spectacular manner, totality, and finality. When Peter spoke of the judgment that took place at Sodom and Gomorrah, turning it to ashes, it was to foreshadow the coming future eschatological judgment by fire."

Journal of the Adventist Theological Society, "Sodom and Gomorrah from an Eschatological Perspective"

The Fire from Heaven

The brimstone and fire that consumed Sodom came directly from the Lord out of heaven. This supernatural destruction prefigures the final conflagration that will consume the present world. As the Apostle Peter teaches:

"But the heavens and the earth which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of the ungodly men... But the day of the Lord shall come as a thief, in which the heavens shall pass away with great violence, and the elements shall be melted with heat, and the earth and the works which are in it, shall be burnt up."

2 Peter 3:7, 10 (Douay-Rheims)

Just as God preserved Noah in the flood and Lot in the fire, He will preserve His elect in the final judgment. As Peter continues: "The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be tormented" (2 Pet 2:9).

The Separation of the Righteous

Before judgment fell, Lot and his family were removed from Sodom. The angels physically led them out, grasping their hands to ensure their escape. This prefigures the gathering of the elect before the final judgment. As our Lord teaches:

"And he shall send his angels with a trumpet, and a great voice: and they shall gather together his elect from the four winds, from the farthest parts of the heavens to the utmost bounds of them."

Matthew 24:31 (Douay-Rheims)

The angels who rescued Lot from Sodom are types of the angels who will rescue the elect from the destruction of this world. As St. Gregory of Nyssa teaches regarding divine judgment:

"God has his reasons for acting in history and while we may not understand why he acted thusly, as in the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, he is always acting in such a way that will bring about the highest good of the creature."

St. Gregory of Nyssa, On the Making of Man

Remember Lot's Wife

Our Lord's command to "remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32) is given in an explicitly eschatological context. He is teaching about the day of His return and warning against attachment to worldly things when that day arrives:

"In that day, he that shall be on the housetop, and his goods in the house, let him not go down to take them away: and he that shall be in the field, in like manner, let him not return back. Remember Lot's wife."

Luke 17:31-32 (Douay-Rheims)

Lot's wife stands as a permanent memorial warning against looking back with longing to this passing world when the eternal world is at hand. At the moment of final judgment, there will be no time for regret or second thoughts. Those who hesitate, who look back, will share her fate.

The Two Cities

St. Augustine's great work The City of God finds in the Sodom narrative a contrast between the city of man and the city of God. Sodom represents the earthly city in its fullest corruption: proud, wealthy, violent, and hostile to the messengers of God. Its destruction is both historical judgment and eschatological sign.

The faithful, like Lot, must live as pilgrims in the earthly city while their true citizenship is in heaven. They may be vexed daily by the wickedness around them, but they must maintain their faith until deliverance comes. The Book of Revelation picks up this imagery when it describes the "great city, which spiritually is called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord also was crucified" (Rev 11:8).

The Offspring of the Saved

Despite the troubling circumstances of their conception, the sons born to Lot's daughters would play a role in salvation history. Ruth the Moabitess became an ancestress of King David and ultimately of Christ Himself. This demonstrates that God's providence works even through human failure and sin to accomplish His saving purposes.

The anagogical lesson is one of hope: even from the ruins of judgment, God brings forth new life. Even from the most troubled origins, God can raise up children of the promise. The line that began in a cave outside destroyed Sodom would lead ultimately to Bethlehem and to the Savior of the world.

The Eternal Example

Jude calls Sodom and Gomorrah an example (deigma) of eternal fire. The word suggests not merely a warning but a visible demonstration, an ongoing proof of what awaits the ungodly. The desolation of the Dead Sea region, where these cities once stood, serves as a perpetual memorial of divine judgment.

"As Sodom and Gomorrha, and the neighbouring cities, in like manner, having given themselves to fornication, and going after other flesh, were made an example, suffering the punishment of eternal fire."

Jude 1:7 (Douay-Rheims)

The phrase "suffering the punishment of eternal fire" indicates that Sodom's judgment points beyond itself to the eternal consequences of unrepentant sin. The temporal fire that consumed these cities is a figure of the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels, into which the wicked will be cast at the last judgment.

The Hope of Deliverance

Yet the anagogical sense is not only about judgment but also about hope. Lot was delivered. The righteous will not perish with the wicked. God knows how to rescue the godly from trial while reserving the ungodly for punishment. This is the great consolation of the faithful in every age: though the world around them may be ripe for judgment, they need not fear, for their deliverance is certain.

The final vision of Scripture is not of destruction but of the new heavens and new earth, the holy city descending from God, where He will dwell with His people forever. The judgment of Sodom, terrible as it was, clears the way for the promise: "Behold, I make all things new" (Rev 21:5). Those who flee from sin and do not look back will inherit this eternal city, where there is no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain.
